claim: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is driven by dysfunction between host genetics, the microbiota, and immune system.
source: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is driven by dysfunction between host genetics, the microbiota, and immune system.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding of IBD pathogenesis.

claim: The Crohn's disease risk allele ATG16L1 T300A results in abnormal Paneth cells due to decreased selective autophagy.
source: The Crohn's disease risk allele ATG16L1 T300A results in abnormal Paneth cells due to decreased selective autophagy, increased cytokine release, and decreased intracellular bacterial clearance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on ATG16L1 T300A function.

claim: The Crohn's disease risk allele ATG16L1 T300A results in increased cytokine release.
source: The Crohn's disease risk allele ATG16L1 T300A results in abnormal Paneth cells due to decreased selective autophagy, increased cytokine release, and decreased intracellular bacterial clearance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on ATG16L1 T300A function.

claim: The Crohn's disease risk allele ATG16L1 T300A results in decreased intracellular bacterial clearance.
source: The Crohn's disease risk allele ATG16L1 T300A results in abnormal Paneth cells due to decreased selective autophagy, increased cytokine release, and decreased intracellular bacterial clearance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on ATG16L1 T300A function.

claim: ATG16L1 T300A mice show increases in Bacteroides ovatus.
source: We observed increases in Bacteroides ovatus and Th1 and Th17 cells in ATG16L1 T300A mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with T300A knock-in mice.

claim: ATG16L1 T300A mice show increases in Th1 cells.
source: We observed increases in Bacteroides ovatus and Th1 and Th17 cells in ATG16L1 T300A mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with T300A knock-in mice.

claim: ATG16L1 T300A mice show increases in Th17 cells.
source: We observed increases in Bacteroides ovatus and Th1 and Th17 cells in ATG16L1 T300A mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with T300A knock-in mice.

claim: Association of altered Schaedler flora mice with B. ovatus specifically increased Th17 cells selectively in ATG16L1 T300A knock-in mice.
source: Association of altered Schaedler flora mice with B. ovatus specifically increased Th17 cells selectively in ATG16L1 T300A knock-in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with ASF mice and B. ovatus.

claim: Changes in microbiota and immune infiltration occur before disease onset in ATG16L1 T300A mice.
source: Changes occur before disease onset, suggesting that ATG16L1 T300A contributes to dysbiosis and immune infiltration prior to disease symptoms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's observations in gnotobiotic mice that showed no histological disease.

claim: ATG16L1 T300A contributes to dysbiosis prior to disease symptoms.
source: Changes occur before disease onset, suggesting that ATG16L1 T300A contributes to dysbiosis and immune infiltration prior to disease symptoms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's observations in gnotobiotic mice.

claim: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are characterized by chronic relapsing inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), the two main forms of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), are characterized by chronic relapsing inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract (Podolsky, 2002; Turpin et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on IBD.

claim: Host genetics, the gut microbiota and environmental exposures all contribute to IBD pathogenesis.
source: The etiology of IBD is complex, as host genetics, the gut microbiota and environmental exposures all contribute to disease pathogenesis (Xavier and Podolsky, 2007; Garrett et al., 2010a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on IBD etiology.

claim: A breakdown in the ability of a genetically susceptible host to respond appropriately to the gut microbiota may lead to an overactive local immune response.
source: A breakdown in the ability of a genetically susceptible host to respond appropriately to the gut microbiota may lead to an overactive local immune response (Sartor, 2008; Eckburg and Relman, 2007) initiating the chronic cycle of intestinal inflammation core to IBD.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on host-microbiota interactions in IBD.

claim: Many genes within IBD loci are directly involved in pathways controlling the sensing and innate responses to bacteria.
source: Many genes within IBD loci are directly involved in pathways controlling the sensing and innate responses to bacteria (Xavier and Podolsky, 2007; Jostins et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to genome-wide association studies.

claim: There is an absence of intestinal inflammation in several gnotobiotic mouse models of spontaneous colitis maintained under germ-free housing conditions.
source: The relatively longstanding observation that there is an absence of intestinal inflammation in several gnotobiotic mouse models of spontaneous colitis maintained under germ-free housing conditions supports this idea (Elson et al., 2005; Sellon et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on germ-free mouse models.

claim: Diversion of the fecal stream greatly improves symptoms in IBD patients.
source: Furthermore, data from IBD patients demonstrating that diversion of the fecal stream greatly improves symptoms (Rutgeerts et al., 1991; McIlrath, 1971) as well as reduces inflammatory cytokine levels (Daferera et al., 2015) also lends plausibility to this concept.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Diversion of the fecal stream reduces inflammatory cytokine levels in IBD patients.
source: Furthermore, data from IBD patients demonstrating that diversion of the fecal stream greatly improves symptoms (Rutgeerts et al., 1991; McIlrath, 1971) as well as reduces inflammatory cytokine levels (Daferera et al., 2015) also lends plausibility to this concept.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota has been associated with IBD.
source: Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota, including alterations in frequency, diversity and richness of microbial populations (Manichanh et al., 2006; Ott et al., 2004), has been associated with IBD (Morgan et al., 2012; Frank et al., 2007; Willing et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior microbiome studies in IBD.

claim: A reduction in the abundance of the phylum Firmicutes has been associated with IBD.
source: For example, a reduction in the abundance of the phylum Firmicutes, including the genus Clostridium (Rajilić-Stojanović et al., 2013) as well as Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria, has been associated with IBD (Frank et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior microbiome studies.

claim: There is variation in the abundance of Bacteroides in IBD.
source: In contrast, there is variation in the abundance of Bacteroides in IBD (Swidsinski et al., 2002; Swidsinski et al., 2005; Gophna et al., 2006; Rehman et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2016), including an increase in Bacteroides fragilis (Swidsinski et al., 2005; Gophna et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior microbiome studies showing conflicting results.

claim: There is an increase in Bacteroides fragilis in IBD.
source: In contrast, there is variation in the abundance of Bacteroides in IBD (Swidsinski et al., 2002; Swidsinski et al., 2005; Gophna et al., 2006; Rehman et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2016), including an increase in Bacteroides fragilis (Swidsinski et al., 2005; Gophna et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior microbiome studies.

claim: Ruminococcus gnavus is able to thrive in the high levels of oxidative stress in the inflamed gut.
source: Additionally, certain microbes, including Ruminococcus gnavus, are able to thrive in the high levels of oxidative stress in the inflamed gut and are associated with increased disease activity (Hall et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research on R. gnavus.

claim: Ruminococcus gnavus is associated with increased disease activity in IBD.
source: Additionally, certain microbes, including Ruminococcus gnavus, are able to thrive in the high levels of oxidative stress in the inflamed gut and are associated with increased disease activity (Hall et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Fecal levels of secreted proteins are associated with microbiome composition.
source: A population-based metagenomics analysis found associations between fecal levels of secreted proteins and microbiome composition (Zhernakova et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior metagenomics study.

claim: The unique ileal transcriptome of CD patients is associated with alterations in Firmicutes.
source: Additionally, the unique ileal transcriptome of CD patients is associated with alterations in Firmicutes (Haberman et al., 2014), implicating a role for genetics in shaping the microbiota.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior transcriptome study.

claim: Host genetic variants play a role in microbial dysbiosis.
source: Genome wide association studies have shown that host genetic variants play a role in microbial dysbiosis (Hall et al., 2017b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior GWAS studies.

claim: Microbial changes have been observed prior to onset of disease symptoms in IBD.
source: Further supporting the idea that these microbial alterations could be the driving force behind the immune response, microbial changes have been observed prior to onset of disease symptoms and specific microbiota signatures are associated with disease location (Imhann et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior longitudinal study.

claim: Specific microbiota signatures are associated with disease location in IBD.
source: Further supporting the idea that these microbial alterations could be the driving force behind the immune response, microbial changes have been observed prior to onset of disease symptoms and specific microbiota signatures are associated with disease location (Imhann et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Over 230 genetic risk loci have been linked to increased IBD risk.
source: Genome-wide association studies have linked over 230 genetic risk loci to increased IBD risk (Jostins et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015; de Lange et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple GWAS studies.

claim: The microbiota and disease severity have been linked to genetic risk in IBD.
source: The microbiota and disease severity have also been linked to genetic risk (Moustafa et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Genetics can affect the composition of the human gut microbiome.
source: Genetics can affect the composition of the human gut microbiome (Hall et al., 2017b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: IBD is associated with a variety of risk alleles that affect immune activation in response to microbial recognition and handling.
source: Additionally, IBD is associated with a variety of risk alleles that affect immune activation in response to microbial recognition and handling (Davies and Abreu, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior review.

claim: The presence of multiple NOD2 variants is linked to increased levels of Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Many studies have linked IBD to genetic risk variants in NOD2 (Turpin et al., 2018), which is involved in recognition of bacterial muramyl dipeptide, but one study has linked the presence of multiple NOD2 variants to increased levels of Enterobacteriaceae (Knights et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: A single nucleotide polymorphism in ATG16L1 (re2241880, Thr300Ala) is associated with an increased risk of CD.
source: A single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in ATG16L1 (re2241880, Thr300Ala) is associated with an increased risk of CD (Hampe et al., 2007; Rioux et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: ATG16L1 functions in autophagy, a cellular recycling system that aids in the sequestration of intracellular bacteria.
source: ATG16L1 functions in autophagy, a cellular recycling system that aids in the sequestration of intracellular bacteria (Cooney et al., 2010; Travassos et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on ATG16L1 function.

claim: ATG16L1 hypomorphic mice have defects in anti-microbial peptide secretion by Paneth cells.
source: ATG16L1 hypomorphic mice have defects in anti-microbial peptide secretion by Paneth cells (Cadwell et al., 2008) and ATG16L1-deficient macrophages show increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Saitoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior mouse study.

claim: ATG16L1-deficient macrophages show increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: ATG16L1 hypomorphic mice have defects in anti-microbial peptide secretion by Paneth cells (Cadwell et al., 2008) and ATG16L1-deficient macrophages show increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Saitoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior cell study.

claim: Conditional deletion of ATG16L1 specifically in epithelial cells reduces autophagy.
source: Conditional deletion of ATG16L1 specifically in epithelial cells reduces autophagy and renders mice more susceptible to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium infection and systemic translocation (Conway et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior mouse study.

claim: Conditional deletion of ATG16L1 specifically in epithelial cells renders mice more susceptible to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium infection and systemic translocation.
source: Conditional deletion of ATG16L1 specifically in epithelial cells reduces autophagy and renders mice more susceptible to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium infection and systemic translocation (Conway et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior mouse study.

claim: The Thr300Ala (T300A) variant displays enhanced degradation via active caspase 3.
source: The Thr300Ala (T300A) variant displays enhanced degradation via active caspase 3 resulting in a reduction in the levels of ATG16L1 protein and reduced levels of autophagic flux (Murthy et al., 2014; Lassen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: The T300A variant results in a reduction in the levels of ATG16L1 protein.
source: The Thr300Ala (T300A) variant displays enhanced degradation via active caspase 3 resulting in a reduction in the levels of ATG16L1 protein and reduced levels of autophagic flux (Murthy et al., 2014; Lassen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: The T300A variant results in reduced levels of autophagic flux.
source: The Thr300Ala (T300A) variant displays enhanced degradation via active caspase 3 resulting in a reduction in the levels of ATG16L1 protein and reduced levels of autophagic flux (Murthy et al., 2014; Lassen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: NOD2 interacts with ATG16L1.
source: Moreover, microbial signatures are associated with variants in the gene for NOD2 (Xavier and Podolsky, 2007), which interacts with ATG16L1 (Sartor, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: T300A knock-in mice display defects in Paneth cells and goblet cells.
source: T300A knock-in mice display defects in Paneth cells and goblet cells (Lassen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior mouse study.

claim: T300A directly affects lysozyme secretion from Paneth cells in mice in the context of infection.
source: More recently, T300A has been shown to directly affect lysozyme secretion from Paneth cells in mice in the context of infection (Bel et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent mouse study.

claim: A dysfunctional response to the microbiota can lead to adaptive immune cell infiltration in the gut during colitis.
source: A dysfunctional response to the microbiota can lead to adaptive immune cell infiltration in the gut during colitis (Feng et al., 2010; Lodes et al., 2004) and is a key contributor to disease pathology.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Th1 cells play a role in CD.
source: Initially, studies suggested a role for Th1 cells in CD (Parronchi et al., 1997) whereas Th2 cells were viewed as responsible for inflammation in UC (Inoue et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Th2 cells were viewed as responsible for inflammation in UC.
source: Initially, studies suggested a role for Th1 cells in CD (Parronchi et al., 1997) whereas Th2 cells were viewed as responsible for inflammation in UC (Inoue et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Th17 cells are characterized by the expression of the transcription factor RORγt+.
source: Th17 cells are characterized by the expression of the transcription factor RORγt+ and produce high levels of the cytokines IL-17 and IL-22.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Th17 cell biology.

claim: Th17 cells produce high levels of the cytokines IL-17 and IL-22.
source: Th17 cells are characterized by the expression of the transcription factor RORγt+ and produce high levels of the cytokines IL-17 and IL-22.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Th17 cell biology.

claim: High levels of IL-17 and IL-22 have been found in the gut mucosa of CD patients as compared to healthy controls.
source: High levels of these cytokines have been found in the gut mucosa of CD patients as compared to healthy controls (Fujino et al., 2003; Andoh et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: IFN-γ, IL-17 and IL-22 are increased in the affected ileum compared to the uninfected ileum of CD patients.
source: More recently, IFN-γ, a Th1 cell cytokine, IL-17 and IL-22 have been shown to be increased in the affected ileum compared to the uninfected ileum of CD patients (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent clinical study.

claim: T300A conventionally-housed SPF mice display altered gut microbial composition at steady state compared to WT mice.
source: We observed overall alterations in the microbiota of T300A mice compared to WT mice (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: WT and T300A SPF mice showed distinct separation by t-SNE analysis.
source: WT and T300A mice showed distinct separation by t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) analysis (Figure 1b)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: There is an increase in the order Bacteroidales in T300A SPF mice compared to WT mice.
source: we saw an increase in the order Bacteroidales (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: T300A conventionally-housed mice display a decrease in the phylum Firmicutes during gut inflammation compared to WT mice.
source: We observed a decrease in the phylum Firmicutes and an increase in the phyla Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, and Cyanobacteria in T300A mice as compared to WT mice (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing after DSS treatment shown in Figure 2a.

claim: T300A conventionally-housed mice display an increase in the phyla Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, and Cyanobacteria during gut inflammation compared to WT mice.
source: We observed a decrease in the phylum Firmicutes and an increase in the phyla Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, and Cyanobacteria in T300A mice as compared to WT mice (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing after DSS treatment shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The microbiota of WT mice separated from cage-matched T300A mice by t-SNE analysis after DSS treatment.
source: The microbiota of WT mice separated from cage-matched T300A mice by t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) analysis (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There is an increased abundance of the phylum Bacteroidetes in T300A mice compared to WT mice after DSS treatment.
source: When we looked specifically at the phyla Bacteroidetes, there was an increased abundance in T300A mice compared to WT mice (Figure 2c)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: B. ovatus was increased significantly in T300A mice compared to WT mice after DSS treatment.
source: In particular, B. ovatus was increased significantly in T300A mice (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: There is increased glycosaminoglycan degradation in samples from T300A mice after DSS treatment.
source: We analyzed the data using PICRUSt in order to infer metabolic function and found increased glycosaminoglycan degradation in samples from T300A mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from PICRUSt analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glycosaminoglycan degradation is uniquely attributed to Bacteroidetes.
source: a process which is uniquely attributed to Bacteroidetes (Koropatkin et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: T300A mice showed increased weight loss from day 8 through 13 following treatment with DSS compared to WT mice.
source: Additionally, we also observed increased weight loss in T300A mice from day 8 through 13 following treatment with DSS compared to WT mice, suggesting that these alterations in the microbiota are associated with heightened disease susceptibility (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the DSS treatment experiment shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Samples from gnotobiotic mice associated with human stool maintained diversity based on patient disease status by PCA analysis.
source: We observed that samples from these mice maintained diversity based on patient disease status by PCA analysis (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Individual mice associated with the same patient stool clustered together with the original samples from human donor samples.
source: Individual mice associated with the same patient stool clustered together with the original samples from human donor samples used for the GF associations.
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There is a difference in WT vs. T300A mice by PCA in mice that received stool from a CD patient with active disease.
source: We observed a difference in WT vs. T300A mice by PCA in mice that received stool from a CD patient with active disease but not in mice inoculated with stool from a UC patient with active disease (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There is no difference in WT vs. T300A mice by PCA in mice inoculated with stool from a UC patient with active disease.
source: We observed a difference in WT vs. T300A mice by PCA in mice that received stool from a CD patient with active disease but not in mice inoculated with stool from a UC patient with active disease (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There is an increase in the genus Bacteroides in T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD as compared to WT mice.
source: When we examined the microbial composition of WT vs. T300A mice associated with stool from IBD patients with active disease, we observed an increase in the genus Bacteroides in T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD as compared to WT mice (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: B. ovatus was increased in T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD compared to WT mice.
source: B. ovatus was also increased in T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD (Figure 4b)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: High levels of Bacteroides were observed in mice that received stool from patients with active UC but no significant difference between WT and T300A mice.
source: We did observe high levels of Bacteroides in mice that received stool from patients with active UC but no significant difference between WT and T300A mice (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding from the metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There is a trend toward an increase in the genus Bacteroides in IBD patients with T300A (GG) genotype compared to WT (AA) genotype.
source: When we compared the microbiota from IBD patients with WT (AA) genotype versus heterozygous patients (AG) versus T300A (GG) genotype, we saw a trend toward an increase in the genus Bacteroides (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of human patient data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: There is a trend toward an increase in the B. fragilis group in IBD patients with T300A genotype.
source: We also observed a trend toward an increase in the B. fragilis group (Figure 5b)
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of human patient data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: There is a significant increase in the species Bacteroides caccae in IBD patients with T300A genotype.
source: and a significant increase in the species Bacteroides caccae (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of human patient data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: There is a decrease in Clostridia in IBD patients with T300A genotype.
source: In contrast, we observed a decrease in Clostridia and an increase in Gammaproteobacteria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of human patient data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is an increase in Gammaproteobacteria in IBD patients with T300A genotype.
source: In contrast, we observed a decrease in Clostridia and an increase in Gammaproteobacteria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of human patient data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of a heterozygous genotype displays an intermediate phenotype with Bacteroides spp.
source: These data show that the presence of T300A has the potential to reconfigure the human microbiota and that the presence of a heterozygous genotype displays an intermediate phenotype with Bacteroides spp
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There are increased frequencies of Th17 cells in the LP of the colon from T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD.
source: We observed increased frequencies of Th17 and Th1 T cells exclusively in the LP of the colon and ileum from T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD (Figure 6a and c)
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a and c.

claim: There are increased frequencies of Th1 cells in the LP of the colon from T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD.
source: We observed increased frequencies of Th17 and Th1 T cells exclusively in the LP of the colon and ileum from T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD (Figure 6a and c)
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a and c.

claim: There are increased frequencies of Th17 cells in the LP of the ileum from T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD.
source: We observed increased frequencies of Th17 and Th1 T cells exclusively in the LP of the colon and ileum from T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD (Figure 6a and c)
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a and c.

claim: There are increased frequencies of Th1 cells in the LP of the ileum from T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD.
source: We observed increased frequencies of Th17 and Th1 T cells exclusively in the LP of the colon and ileum from T300A mice that received stool from patients with active CD (Figure 6a and c)
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a and c.

claim: There are no increased frequencies of Th17 and Th1 T cells in the LP of the colon or ileum of mice that received stool from patients with active UC.
source: and not in the LP of the colon or ileum of mice that received stool from patients with active UC (Figure 6b and d).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6b and d.

claim: There is an increase in the frequency of Tregs in the LP of the colon from T300A mice associated with stool from patients with CD.
source: We also found an increase in the frequency of Tregs in the LP of the colon from T300A mice associated with stool from patients with CD (Figure 6a)
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: There is a minor increase in Tregs in the ileum in T300A mice associated with stool from patients with UC.
source: and a minor increase in the ileum in T300A mice associated with stool from patients with UC (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: There is a reduced frequency of conventional DCs in the LP of the colon from T300A mice associated with stool from patients with active CD.
source: We saw a reduced frequency of conventional DCs and a slight increase in the frequency of tolerogenic DCs along with a decrease in neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes in T300A mice (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: There is a slight increase in the frequency of tolerogenic DCs in the LP of the colon from T300A mice associated with stool from patients with active CD.
source: We saw a reduced frequency of conventional DCs and a slight increase in the frequency of tolerogenic DCs along with a decrease in neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes in T300A mice (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: There is a decrease in neutrophils in the LP of the colon from T300A mice associated with stool from patients with active CD.
source: We saw a reduced frequency of conventional DCs and a slight increase in the frequency of tolerogenic DCs along with a decrease in neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes in T300A mice (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: There is a decrease in inflammatory monocytes in the LP of the colon from T300A mice associated with stool from patients with active CD.
source: We saw a reduced frequency of conventional DCs and a slight increase in the frequency of tolerogenic DCs along with a decrease in neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes in T300A mice (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Histology-based grading of the colon and small intestine from mice associated with human IBD stool showed no signs of colitis, enteritis, or any intestinal histopathology.
source: It should be noted that histology-based grading of the colon and small intestine from mice associated with human IBD stool showed no signs of colitis, enteritis, or any intestinal histopathology (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: T300A ASF mice associated with B. ovatus 8483 showed an increase only in Th17 cells in the LP of the colon.
source: However, T300A ASF mice showed an increase only in Th17 cells in the LP of the colon and ileum when B. ovatus 8483 was present (Figure 8b and d)
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 8b and d.

claim: T300A ASF mice associated with B. ovatus 8483 showed an increase only in Th17 cells in the LP of the ileum.
source: However, T300A ASF mice showed an increase only in Th17 cells in the LP of the colon and ileum when B. ovatus 8483 was present (Figure 8b and d)
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 8b and d.

claim: There was no difference in Th17 cells in ASF mice in the absence of B. ovatus 8483.
source: but there was no difference in ASF mice in the absence of B. ovatus 8483 (Figure 8a and c).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 8a and c.

claim: There is a slight decrease in Th1 cells in the ileum of T300A ASF mice in the presence of B. ovatus 8483.
source: Besides a slight decrease in Th1 cells in the ileum of T300A ASF mice in the presence of B. ovatus 8483 (Figure 8d), there were no other changes in the immune populations analyzed.
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 8d.

claim: The increase in frequency of Th17 cells in T300A ASF mice with B. ovatus 8483 occurred in the absence of colitis, enteritis, or any intestinal histopathology.
